content: Lichen nitidus is a chronic inflammatory skin condition of unknown cause. It is characterized by small, discrete, uniform papules measuring 1-2 mm in diameter. These papules are shiny, flat-topped, and can appear pale flesh-colored or reddish-brown. In individuals with darker skin tones, the papules may appear hypopigmented. Occasionally, minimal scaling may be present or can be induced by rubbing the surface of the lesions. This condition typically affects children and young adults. It is generally painless and non-itchy, although prolonged itching (pruritus) may occur in some cases. The papules often appear in linear arrangements, a phenomenon known as the Koebner phenomenon, particularly on the forearms. In some cases, the papules may be grouped together but do not merge into larger lesions. They are most commonly localized to areas such as the chest, abdomen, glans penis, and the flexor surfaces of the upper extremities. Less commonly, the condition may present in two distinct patterns: In these cases, the papules may merge into erythematous plaques with minimal scaling, and the redness may develop shades of violet, brown, or yellow. Histologically, lichen nitidus is characterized by a localized granulomatous lymphohistiocytic infiltrate within an expanded dermal papilla. The overlying epidermis is thinned, and the rete ridges extend downward at the lateral margins of the infiltrate, creating a distinctive claw clutching a ball appearance under the microscope. In terms of diagnosis, physical examination of the skin is crucial. The characteristic appearance of the papules, along with their distribution and histological findings, aids in confirming the diagnosis. Treatment is generally not required for lichen nitidus, as it is often asymptomatic and self-limiting. However, if persistent itching is present or if the appearance of the lesions significantly impacts the patient’s quality of life, topical glucocorticoids may be used. In cases where the disease is symptomatic, generalized, and extensive, oral glucocorticoids may be considered. Other treatment options that have been reported include PUVA therapy, UVA/UVB phototherapy, and systemic agents such as astemizole, acitretin, and etretinate.
